near_miss.lead: White as snow: hvitt sem snior
near_miss.why_not: Searched snow forms across corpora, then Greek lemma χιών. Homer Il. 10.437 has λευκότεροι χιόνος, but neither lexical item is cognate with the Norse pair; the comparison concerns horses rather than a sail and is an obvious independently available simile. The slab partners do not preserve it. No inherited phrase claimed.

near_miss.lead: Seeing the whole world before one’s eyes
near_miss.why_not: Read as a Christian royal vision. The Greek partner’s μέτωπον describes the face of a rectangular city, not visionary sight; shared eye-derived material supplies no parallel phrase.

Norse vega with a human object is generic killing language; Sanskrit uses han and vīra, not the same lexical pair. Russian везеть refers to carrying fetters; its transport verb must not be equated with the Norse slaying verb.

Norse liggja and Russian лежати are cognate, as are nátt and нощь, but night is merely a time adjunct in routine lodging narratives. The Christian prayer vigil and Itlar’s overnight lodging do not establish a distinctive shared figure or formula.

near_miss.lead: Sleep and night; the wakeful vigil
near_miss.why_not: Searched night plus sleep roots and read 15 saga hits. These are routine sleeping, sleeplessness and dream reports. Homer has an epithet sleepless modifying nights, whereas Norse contrasts the king praying with other men falling asleep. Cognate nouns do not share the relevant syntax or the same distinctive context.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_2_11_Agathangelos ed. page 1495 - PDF page 201 (word id 35266)
near_miss.why_not: Norse yrkja describes composition; the Greek and Armenian cognate work vocabulary concerns deeds, and no second shared term forms a poetic making collocation. The Armenian passage is also explicitly theological.

near_miss.lead: Daughter and sister in paired kinship identifications
near_miss.why_not: Both kinship terms are cognate, but Norse supplies ordinary royal genealogy, whereas the Atharvan passage gives a ritual object personified parentage and sibling status. The obvious relations do not warrant reconstructing a formula.

near_miss.lead: Binding the foot; bond and step
near_miss.why_not: Norse describes treating a horse’s injured legs. Sanskrit contrasts release from birth’s bondage with reaching an unharmed state; bandha and pada are not a bind-the-foot construction. Root overlap is insufficient.

near_miss.lead: Dogs and men in an encompassing list
near_miss.why_not: Irish gives an explicit repeated-between merism, with coin accusative plural of cú and gilla denoting attendants. Norse hundr belongs to Þórir’s byname, while menn is the object of killing. The Norse passage contains no matching merism.

Searched ahi with han and read AVŚ 2.5.s10-11 and AVP 12.12.s2, among other hits. They provide actual serpent-slaying wording, unlike the retrieved Latin/Russian partners. But Norse vega and ormr renew both terms relative to han and ahi; the slab Atharvan serpent passage describes the slain serpent lying like cut branches, not the Norse wording. The famous comparison is recalled from the literature; thematic continuity alone is insufficient for a phrase claim here.

note: All bundles read in order in sections. No defensible inherited phrase claims. Recorded 10 near-misses and 18 error reports; corpus searches tested snow comparisons, sleep/night collocations and serpent-slaying. No search lead with sufficient cognate phrase material accepted.
